content: 1. Administer one full applicator of the 3% intravaginal gel as a single dose at bedtime. 2. The safety and efficacy of this medication have not been established in patients under 12 years of age. 3. Do not use this medication in combination with other vaginal products, as it may alter the release of progesterone. 4. Avoid coadministration of metronidazole vaginal gel with the cholera vaccine due to potential pharmacodynamic antagonism. 5. Systemic antibiotics may interfere with the cholera vaccine strain; avoid administering the vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 6. Metronidazole vaginal gel may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 7. Disulfiram increases the toxicity of metronidazole vaginal gel by inhibiting its metabolism, potentially leading to enhanced central nervous system (CNS) and cardiac toxicity. This is less likely with vaginal administration due to lower systemic absorption. 8. Metronidazole vaginal gel may increase the effects of ethanol by reducing its metabolism, potentially causing a disulfiram-like reaction (e.g., abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, flushing). This reaction is less likely with vaginal administration. 9. Severe, irreversible hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure, including fatal outcomes, have been reported in patients with Cockayne syndrome after initiating metronidazole or related nitroimidazole drugs. 10. Metronidazole is contraindicated in patients with Cockayne syndrome, those who have taken disulfiram within the past two weeks, and those consuming alcohol or products containing propylene glycol within at least three days of treatment. 11. Oral and intravenous administration of metronidazole has been associated with seizures, encephalopathy, aseptic meningitis, and peripheral neuropathy. 12. Metronidazole has been shown to be carcinogenic in mice and rats; avoid unnecessary use. 13. Metronidazole may interfere with laboratory assessments of AST, ALT, LDH, triglycerides, and glucose hexokinase. 14. There are no data on the use of intravaginal metronidazole in pregnant women. 15. Metronidazole is present in human milk following oral administration at concentrations similar to plasma levels. Vaginal administration achieves only 2% of the mean maximum serum concentration of a 500 mg oral dose. 16. Breastfeeding mothers should weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. Alternatively, they may interrupt breastfeeding, pump and discard breast milk during treatment and for 48 hours after the last dose, and feed the infant stored human milk or formula. 17. Animal studies have shown tumorigenicity with chronic oral administration of metronidazole in rats and mice, but the clinical relevance of these findings is unclear. 18. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk, making the drug generally acceptable for use during pregnancy. 19. The pharmacokinetics of metronidazole vaginal gel indicate a peak plasma concentration of 281 ng/mL (2% of the oral dose) and an AUC of 125,000 ng•hr/mL (5% of a single oral dose). 20. Patients should consult their healthcare provider for the most current information regarding formulary status and drug interactions.
